title: Applied Twice
statement: Let $\pi$ be a permutation of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, 12\}$, chosen uniformly at random from all $12!$ permutations. For a subset $S$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, 12\}$, write $\pi^2(S) = \{\pi(\pi(s)) : s \in S\}$. The probability that no nonempty subset $S$ with $|S| \le 3$ satisfies $\pi^2(S) = S$ is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m + n$.
hints: Take an element $s$ of a set $S$ with $\pi^2(S) = S$. Which other elements are forced into $S$? Work out what the smallest possible sets of this kind look like.

Use the cycle decomposition. A set with $\pi^2(S) = S$ is a union of cycles of $\pi^2$, so the condition says that every cycle of $\pi^2$ has length at least $4$. To see what squaring does to an $l$-cycle of $\pi$, model that cycle as the map $x \mapsto x + 1$ on the integers modulo $l$, so that $\pi^2$ acts as $x \mapsto x + 2$.

Under squaring, an odd $l$-cycle stays a single $l$-cycle, and an even $l$-cycle splits into two cycles of length $\frac{l}{2}$. So the cycles of $\pi$ must have odd length at least $5$ or even length at least $8$. The only ways to write $12$ as a sum of such lengths are $12$ and $7 + 5$. Now find the proportion of permutations with each of these two cycle types.
solution:
A nonempty $S$ with $\pi^2(S)=S$ contains, with each $s$, the whole $\pi^2$-cycle of $s$, so it is a union of cycles of $\pi^2$. Conversely, each cycle of $\pi^2$ is such a set. Hence the condition holds exactly when every cycle of $\pi^2$ has length at least $4$.

Take an $l$-cycle of $\pi$ and label it by $\mathbb{Z}_l$, so that $\pi^2$ is $x\mapsto x+2$. For odd $l$ this is a single $l$-cycle. For even $l$ it splits into two cycles of length $\frac{l}{2}$. So the allowed lengths $l$ are the odd $l\ge 5$ and the even $l\ge 8$, that is $5,7,8,9,10,11,12$.

The lengths sum to $12$ and each is at least $5$, so there are at most two cycles. One cycle gives a $12$-cycle. Two cycles have lengths $5+7$ or $6+6$, and $6$ is not allowed, so only $5+7$ remains.

The number of $12$-cycles is $11!$, a proportion $\frac{1}{12}$. The number of permutations of type $5+7$ is
$$\binom{12}{5}\cdot 4!\cdot 6!=\dfrac{12!}{5!\,7!}\cdot 4!\cdot 6!=\dfrac{12!}{35},$$
a proportion $\frac{1}{35}$. The two types are disjoint, so the probability is
$$\dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{1}{35}=\dfrac{47}{420}.$$

Since $47$ is prime and does not divide $420$, the fraction is in lowest terms. Thus $m+n=47+420=467$.
